```{r helpers, include=FALSE}
# ============================================================
# Helper: render a data frame as a table IMAGE
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Why: text output from print() is split by knitr into many small
# "##" boxes, which is hard to read. Rendering the table as a
# graphic gives one clean, aligned table per question.
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# transpose = TRUE  -> first column becomes the column names and the
#                      remaining columns are transposed, so that each
#                      statistic becomes a row (good for wide tables
#                      such as summary statistics of several series).
tab_fig <- function(df, title = "", transpose = TRUE,
                    digits = 4, base_size = 8) {
  df <- as.data.frame(df)
  for (j in seq_along(df)) {
    if (is.numeric(df[[j]])) df[[j]] <- round(df[[j]], digits)
  }

  if (transpose && ncol(df) > 1 && !is.numeric(df[[1]])) {
    rn <- as.character(df[[1]])
    m  <- as.data.frame(t(as.matrix(df[, -1, drop = FALSE])))
    names(m) <- rn
  } else {
    m <- df
  }

  tg <- tableGrob(m, theme = ttheme_minimal(base_size = base_size))

  grid.arrange(
    tg,
    top = if (nzchar(title))
      textGrob(title, gp = gpar(fontsize = 11, fontface = "bold")) else NULL
  )
}

# Helper: print a named numeric vector as ONE single text block
# (avoids knitr splitting the output into several boxes)
show_vec <- function(x, title = "", digits = 4) {
  x <- round(x, digits)
  txt <- paste0("  ", format(names(x), justify = "left"), " = ", as.character(x))
  cat(paste(c(if (nzchar(title)) title, txt, ""), collapse = "\n"))
}
```

# Question 1

## Question 1 (a) and (b)

```{r q1ab}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1(a) Simulate one sample path of  dX_t = dt + 3 dB_t  on the interval [3, 5]
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The SDE is a GENERALISED WIENER PROCESS (arithmetic Brownian motion) with a
# constant drift mu = 1 and a constant diffusion sigma = 3.  Because the
# coefficients do not depend on X_t or on t, the process has the exact solution
#       X_t = X_3 + (t - 3) + 3 (B_t - B_3),
# and therefore the increment over a step of length dt is
#       dX_i ~ i.i.d. N(mu * dt, sigma^2 * dt) = N(dt, 9 dt).
# We simulate those increments directly: this is exact in distribution for any
# finite dt, so the only approximation is the resolution of the time grid.

set.seed(123)                  # reproducibility

t0 <- 3                        # start time
t1 <- 5                        # end time
n  <- 20000                    # number of increments on [3, 5]
dt <- (t1 - t0) / n            # time step = 0.0001
t_grid <- t0 + (0:n) * dt      # time grid t_0, ..., t_n   (n + 1 points)

Z  <- rnorm(n)                 # Z_i ~ N(0, 1)
dX <- dt + 3 * sqrt(dt) * Z    # dX_i = dt + 3 * sqrt(dt) * Z_i  ~ N(dt, 9dt)
X  <- c(1, 1 + cumsum(dX))     # start from X_3 = 1 and accumulate  (n + 1 points)

plot(t_grid, X, type = "l", lwd = 1, col = "grey30",
     xlab = "t", ylab = expression(X[t]),
     main = "Question 1(a),(b): simulated path, theoretical mean and 95% bands")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1(b) Theoretical conditional mean and 95% pointwise bands
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Taking expectation and variance of the exact solution, conditional on X_3:
#       E(X_t | X_3 = 1)   = 1 + (t - 3)
#       Var(X_t | X_3 = 1) = 9 (t - 3)
# The variance grows LINEARLY with elapsed time, so the bands widen as t
# increases - they "fan out" rather than staying parallel.
m     <- 1 + (t_grid - t0)     # conditional mean
v     <- 9 * (t_grid - t0)     # conditional variance
upper <- m + 1.96 * sqrt(v)
lower <- m - 1.96 * sqrt(v)

lines(t_grid, m,     col = "red",  lwd = 2)
lines(t_grid, upper, col = "blue", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
lines(t_grid, lower, col = "blue", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)

legend("topleft",
       legend = c("sample path", "theoretical mean", "pointwise 95% bands"),
       col    = c("grey30", "red", "blue"),
       lty    = c(1, 1, 2),
       lwd    = c(1, 2, 1.5),
       bty    = "n")
```

**Answer (a).** The interval is $[3,5]$ with $n=20000$ equally spaced increments, so the time step is
$\Delta t=(5-3)/20000=0.0001$ and the time grid is $t_i=3+i\Delta t$, $i=0,1,\dots,20000$.
The model is the generalised Brownian motion $dX_t=dt+3\,dB_t$. Over a small interval
$\Delta X_i=X_{t_i}-X_{t_{i-1}}=\Delta t+3\,\Delta B_i$ with
$\Delta B_i\sim N(0,\Delta t)$. Writing $\Delta B_i=\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z_i$, $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$ independent,
gives $\Delta X_i=\Delta t+3\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z_i$, and starting from $X_3=1$ the path is built as
$X_{t_i}=1+\sum_{j=1}^{i}\Delta X_j$. With $\Delta t=10^{-4}$ the simulated path is visually continuous,
as expected since the increments are independent $N(\mu\Delta t,\sigma^2\Delta t)$.

**Answer (b).** Integrating the SDE from $3$ to $t$ gives
$X_t-X_3=(t-3)+3(B_t-B_3)$, hence $X_t=1+(t-3)+3(B_t-B_3)$. Since $B_t-B_3\sim N(0,t-3)$,
$$\mathbb{E}(X_t\mid X_3=1)=t-2,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_t\mid X_3=1)=9(t-3),$$
so $X_t\mid X_3=1\sim N\big(t-2,\,9(t-3)\big)$ [Week 5 §3.4, with $\mu=1$, $\sigma=3$ and elapsed time $t-3$].

The simulated path fluctuates around the theoretical mean line $t-2$, and its deviations from that line widen as $t$ increases. This is because the conditional variance is proportional to elapsed time, $\operatorname{Var}=9(t-3)$,
so the pointwise bands $\pm1.96\sqrt{9(t-3)}$ fan out from $t=3$ to $t=5$. Near $t=3$ the band is very
narrow and the path is almost forced through the mean; by $t=5$ the band is much wider, so a single path may
deviate noticeably from the mean while still lying inside the bands. By construction roughly 95% of the path
lies inside the bands.

## Question 1 (c)

```{r q1c}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1(c) 500 independent paths: the terminal distribution of X_5
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Every path is generated on the SAME time grid as in 1(a); only the random
# shocks differ.  Storing the draws in an n x 500 matrix lets us build all the
# paths with a single call to rnorm() and obtain the terminal values with a
# column sum, which is far faster than a loop over paths.
set.seed(1)                    # a different seed, so these paths differ from (a)
n_paths <- 500

Zmat  <- matrix(rnorm(n * n_paths), nrow = n, ncol = n_paths)  # n x 500 shocks
dXmat <- dt + 3 * sqrt(dt) * Zmat                              # increments
X5    <- 1 + colSums(dXmat)     # terminal value on each path

sim_mean  <- mean(X5)
sim_var   <- var(X5)
theo_mean <- 3                  # E(X_5 | X_3 = 1) = 1 + (5 - 3)
theo_var  <- 18                 # Var(X_5 | X_3 = 1) = 9 * (5 - 3)
theo_sd   <- sqrt(theo_var)

# ---- 95% CI for the mean ----
alpha   <- 0.05
z_crit  <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)
se_mean <- sqrt(theo_var / n_paths)
ci_mean <- c(sim_mean - z_crit * se_mean, sim_mean + z_crit * se_mean)

# ---- 95% CI for the variance (exact chi-square interval) ----
df_var   <- n_paths - 1
chi_low  <- qchisq(alpha / 2,     df_var)
chi_high <- qchisq(1 - alpha / 2, df_var)
ci_var   <- c(df_var * sim_var / chi_high, df_var * sim_var / chi_low)

# ---- Results table as an image ----
res_q1c <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c("Simulated mean", "Simulated variance",
               "Theoretical mean", "Theoretical variance",
               "95% CI for mean (lower)", "95% CI for mean (upper)",
               "95% CI for variance (lower)", "95% CI for variance (upper)"),
  Value = c(sim_mean, sim_var, theo_mean, theo_var,
            ci_mean[1], ci_mean[2], ci_var[1], ci_var[2])
)
tab_fig(res_q1c, title = "Question 1(c): simulated vs theoretical moments of X5",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 4, base_size = 10)

cat("\nTheoretical mean inside its 95% CI?  ",
    ifelse(theo_mean >= ci_mean[1] && theo_mean <= ci_mean[2], "YES", "NO"), "\n")
cat("Theoretical variance inside its 95% CI?  ",
    ifelse(theo_var >= ci_var[1] && theo_var <= ci_var[2], "YES", "NO"), "\n")
```

```{r q1c-hist}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Histogram of the simulated terminal values vs the theoretical density
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Under the model X_5 is EXACTLY normal, so the histogram should follow the
# N(3, 18) curve; any departure is finite-sample simulation error, not model
# error.
hist(X5, probability = TRUE, breaks = 35, col = "lightblue",
     main = "Question 1(c): simulated X5 with theoretical N(3,18) density",
     xlab = expression(X[5]), ylab = "Density")

curve(dnorm(x, mean = theo_mean, sd = theo_sd),
      add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)

legend("topright",
       legend = c("Simulated X5", "Theoretical N(3,18) density"),
       col    = c("lightblue", "red"),
       lwd    = c(10, 2),
       bty    = "n")
```

**Answer (c).** Setting $t=5$ in the expression from part (b):
$X_5=1+2+3(B_5-B_3)=3+3(B_5-B_3)$ with $B_5-B_3\sim N(0,2)$, so $3(B_5-B_3)\sim N(0,18)$ and
$$X_5\mid X_3=1\ \sim\ N(3,\,18).$$
The table above reports the simulated mean and variance of the 500 terminal values alongside the theoretical
values and two 95% confidence intervals: $\bar X\pm1.96\sqrt{18/500}$ for the mean.

The figure shows the histogram of the simulated $X_5$ with the theoretical $N(3,18)$ density superimposed.
The simulated distribution is broadly consistent with the theoretical normal density, although with only 500
paths the histogram is not perfectly smooth and some bins deviate from the curve. Using different random seeds
can occasionally produce a sample mean or variance outside its interval; this reflects simulation error at
$n=500$, and error would diminish with more paths.

# Question 2

```{r q2-helpers, include=FALSE}
# Summary-statistics helper: always returns the same 15 columns
# (so that rbind() across series works)
summ_one <- function(x, name) {
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  data.frame(
    Series = name, N = length(x),
    Mean = mean(x), SD = sd(x), Var = var(x),
    Min = min(x),
    Q1 = as.numeric(quantile(x, 0.25)),
    Median = median(x),
    Q3 = as.numeric(quantile(x, 0.75)),
    Max = max(x),
    Skew = moments::skewness(x),
    Kurt = moments::kurtosis(x),
    Zero = mean(x == 0),
    Neg  = mean(x < 0),
    Pos  = mean(x > 0),
    row.names = NULL
  )
}

# ACF helper
get_acf_tbl <- function(x, name, lag.max = 10) {
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  a <- acf(x, lag.max = lag.max, plot = FALSE)
  out <- as.data.frame(t(as.numeric(a$acf)))
  names(out) <- paste0("lag", as.numeric(a$lag))
  cbind(Series = name, out, row.names = NULL)
}
```

## Question 2 (a)

```{r q2a}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2(a) Within-day 5-minute log returns and the jump contributions J1, J2, J3
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# ECONOMIC BACKGROUND.  Quadratic variation decomposes into a continuous part
# (integrated variance, IV) and a jump part:
#       QV  =  IV  +  sum of squared jumps.
# Realized variance (RV) estimates the whole of QV, whereas bipower variation
# (BV) is built from products of ADJACENT returns and is therefore robust to
# isolated jumps, so it estimates IV alone.  Their difference isolates the jump
# component of variation.
file <- "data/mdtx_intraday_prices.xlsx"

prices_1m  <- read_excel(file, sheet = "1minute")
prices_5m  <- read_excel(file, sheet = "5minute")
prices_30m <- read_excel(file, sheet = "30minute")

# ---- Timestamp handling ---------------------------------------------------
# The raw timestamps are recorded in US Eastern Time (market local time).
# force_tz() attaches the correct zone WITHOUT shifting the clock time, which
# fixes the common artefact of 09:30-16:00 being displayed as 05:30-12:00.
clean_time <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    mutate(
      timestamp = force_tz(as.POSIXct(timestamp), tzone = "America/New_York"),
      date      = as.Date(timestamp, tz = "America/New_York"),
      time      = format(timestamp, "%H:%M:%S", tz = "America/New_York")
    ) %>%
    filter(time >= "09:30:00", time <= "16:00:00")
}

prices_1m  <- clean_time(prices_1m)
prices_5m  <- clean_time(prices_5m)
prices_30m <- clean_time(prices_30m)

# ---- Within-day 5-minute log returns -------------------------------------
# Taking the lag WITHIN each date via group_by(date) drops the first
# observation of every day, so close-to-open overnight returns are excluded.
# This leaves 78 five-minute returns per day (79 prices -> 78 returns).
prices_5m <- prices_5m %>%
  arrange(date, timestamp) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  mutate(lp = log(price), ret5 = lp - lag(lp)) %>%
  ungroup()

check_daily <- prices_5m %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(n_prices  = n(),
            n_returns = sum(!is.na(ret5)),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  as.data.frame(row.names = NULL)

# ---- Jump contributions, built at 5-minute granularity -------------------
#   RV contribution :  r_i^2                        (squared return)
#   BV contribution :  (pi/2) * |r_i| * |r_{i-1}|   (product of ADJACENT returns)
#       The pi/2 factor standardises the product of absolute returns so that it
#       is unbiased under a Gaussian benchmark, and using ADJACENT returns is
#       precisely what makes BV insensitive to isolated jumps.
#   J1 = RV - BV      signed jump variation
#   J2 = max(J1, 0)   the standard empirical convention, since the theoretical
#                     jump variation sum(kappa^2) is non-negative
#   J3 = J1 / RV      relative jump contribution; unstable when RV is small
prices_5m <- prices_5m %>%
  arrange(date, timestamp) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  mutate(
    RV_contrib = ret5^2,
    BV_contrib = (pi / 2) * abs(ret5 * lag(ret5)),
    J1 = RV_contrib - BV_contrib,
    J2 = pmax(RV_contrib - BV_contrib, 0),
    J3 = ifelse(RV_contrib > 0, J1 / RV_contrib, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# ---- Table 1: daily counts ----
tab_fig(check_daily, title = "Table 1. Daily counts of 5-minute prices and returns",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 0, base_size = 9)

# ---- Table 2: summary statistics of J1 / J2 / J3 ----
stats_tbl <- rbind(
  summ_one(prices_5m$J1, "J1"),
  summ_one(prices_5m$J2, "J2"),
  summ_one(prices_5m$J3, "J3")
)
tab_fig(stats_tbl, title = "Table 2. Summary statistics of J1 / J2 / J3",
        digits = 7, base_size = 8)

# ---- Table 3: autocorrelations of J1 and J2 ----
acf_tbl <- rbind(get_acf_tbl(prices_5m$J1, "J1", lag.max = 10),
                 get_acf_tbl(prices_5m$J2, "J2", lag.max = 10))
tab_fig(acf_tbl, title = "Table 3. Autocorrelation of J1 / J2 (lag 0 to lag 10)",
        digits = 7, base_size = 8)

# ---- Table 5: three largest J2 contributions ----
top3_J2 <- prices_5m %>%
  filter(is.finite(J2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(J2)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 3) %>%
  mutate(minutes_from_open = round(as.numeric(difftime(
    timestamp,
    as.POSIXct(paste(date, "09:30:00"), tz = "America/New_York"),
    units = "mins")), 1)) %>%
  mutate(timestamp = format(timestamp, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")) %>%
  select(date, timestamp, price, ret5, J2, minutes_from_open) %>%
  as.data.frame(row.names = NULL)
tab_fig(top3_J2, title = "Table 4. Three largest J2 jump contributions",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 7, base_size = 9)
```

```{r q2a-acf}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Autocorrelation functions of J1 and J2
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# J1 is expected to show a NEGATIVE spike at lag 1: consecutive BV terms share
# one absolute return, |r_i|, so the -BV component introduces mechanical
# negative dependence that has nothing to do with genuine jump clustering.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(na.omit(prices_5m$J1), lag.max = 40, main = "ACF of J1")
acf(na.omit(prices_5m$J2), lag.max = 40, main = "ACF of J2")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r q2a-spike}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Spike plot of the J2 series: WHEN do jumps occur?
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A spike plot (vertical lines from zero) makes the clustering of jump days and
# the long runs of zeros far more visible than a line plot would.
ggplot(prices_5m %>% filter(is.finite(J2)), aes(x = timestamp, y = J2)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = timestamp, yend = 0), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "black") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Figure. Five-minute J2 jump contributions",
       x = "US Eastern Time", y = "J2")
```

**Answer (a).**

**1. Data integrity.** Table 1 shows 10 trading days, each with 79 five-minute prices and 78 five-minute
returns, confirming that overnight (close-to-open) returns have been correctly excluded, as required.

**2. Summary statistics of $J1$ and $J2$.** Table 2 shows that for $J1$ the mean is essentially zero
($1\times10^{-7}$), while skewness is strongly positive (9.094) and kurtosis is extremely high (156.2):
most jump contributions are very small, with a few very large positive values generating a long right tail
. For $J2$, because $J2=\max\{J1,0\}$ truncates negative values at zero, the mean is raised and
skewness (13.877) and kurtosis (249.3) increase further; the remaining features are otherwise consistent
with $J1$, and overall the data behave as expected.

**3.ACF.** Table 3 shows that $J1$ has a clearly negative first-order autocorrelation
(lag 1 = $-0.277$), with all higher lags inside the confidence band; the ACF plot shows the same pronounced
spike at lag 1. All autocorrelations of $J2$ lie inside the band, so $J2$ shows essentially no linear serial
dependence — plausibly because the 63.77% of zeros dilute the linear autocorrelation.

This negative lag-1 autocorrelation of $J1$ is a mechanical by-product of the definition of $BV$, not
evidence of jump clustering. $BV$ is built from products of adjacent returns,
$\mathrm{BV}=\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_i|r_i||r_{i-1}|$, so consecutive $BV$ contributions share the same
$|r_i|$ and are positively correlated. Since $J1$ contains $-BV$, the resulting series inherits a negative
lag-1 dependence. This also explains why the effect appears only at lag 1, and why it disappears in $J2$ once
negative values are truncated.

**4. $J3$.** Since $J3_t=(\mathrm{RV}_t-\mathrm{BV}_t)/\mathrm{RV}_t$, extreme values arise whenever the
denominator $\mathrm{RV}$ is close to zero. Table 2 confirms this: the mean is $-4.27$, the SD is $18.65$, the
minimum is $-377$, skewness is $-13.3$ and kurtosis is $232.9$ — strongly left-skewed with a heavy left
tail. $J3$ is therefore unreliable as a local jump contribution: the instability of the denominator
produces extreme values that cannot be interpreted as a jump proportion.

**5. Three largest $J2$ contributions.** Table 4 identifies them as occurring on 2026-04-28 at 11:55,
2026-04-23 at 09:45 and 2026-04-22 at 10:00. Two of the three occur within the first hour of trading
(09:45 and 10:00, i.e. 15 and 30 minutes after the open) and one later in the morning (11:55); with only three
observations, no stronger inference about intraday timing should be drawn. The spike plot shows clear
clustering — long runs of small, closely spaced contributions alternating with long runs of zeros. This is
not necessarily in conflict with the ACF result, because the spike plot describes the temporal occurrence
of non-zero contributions whereas the ACF measures linear dependence in their numerical values; visual
clustering need not imply significant linear autocorrelation. Finally, 28 April and 23 April clearly stand out
above all other days, whereas the third-largest contribution is not far above the remaining large ones. This
indicates that jump contributions are highly uneven, with a few days dominating the whole sample.

## Question 2 (b)

```{r q2b}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2(b) Tri-power quarticity, 30-minute aggregation and the J1 jump tests
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHY TP?  The J1 statistic is standardised by its own standard deviation, which
# depends on the INTEGRATED QUARTICITY, integral(sigma^4 ds) - a fourth-order
# quantity that is not directly observed.  Tri-power quarticity estimates it, and
# is itself jump-robust because it multiplies THREE adjacent absolute returns:
# only finitely many jumps occur, so the probability that two of any three
# neighbouring returns both contain a jump vanishes as dt -> 0.
mu_43      <- 2^(2/3) * gamma(7/6) / gamma(1/2)   # ~ 0.8308615
mu_43_inv3 <- mu_43^(-3)

prices_5m <- prices_5m %>%
  arrange(date, timestamp) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  mutate(
    TP_contrib = mu_43_inv3 *
                 abs(ret5)^(4/3) *
                 abs(lag(ret5))^(4/3) *
                 abs(lag(ret5, 2))^(4/3)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# ---- Assign 30-minute interval indices (1..13) ----
prices_5m <- prices_5m %>%
  arrange(date, timestamp) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  mutate(
    ret_index  = cumsum(!is.na(ret5)),
    interval30 = ifelse(ret_index == 0, NA_integer_, ceiling(ret_index / 6))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# ---- Check: 13 intervals per day ----
check_intervals <- prices_5m %>%
  filter(!is.na(interval30)) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(n_intervals = n_distinct(interval30), .groups = "drop") %>%
  as.data.frame(row.names = NULL)
tab_fig(check_intervals,
        title = "Table 6. Number of 30-minute intervals per day",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 0, base_size = 9)

# ---- Aggregate 5-minute contributions to 30-minute intervals ----
agg_30 <- prices_5m %>%
  filter(!is.na(interval30)) %>%
  group_by(date, interval30) %>%
  summarise(
    RV = sum(RV_contrib, na.rm = TRUE),
    BV = sum(BV_contrib, na.rm = TRUE),
    TP = sum(TP_contrib, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(J1 = RV - BV)

# ---- One-sided J1 jump test ----
theta <- pi^2 / 4 + pi - 5      # ~ 0.6089938
q95   <- qnorm(0.95)

test_jump <- function(J1_vec, TP_vec) {
  J1_sum <- sum(J1_vec, na.rm = TRUE)
  TP_sum <- sum(TP_vec, na.rm = TRUE)
  z      <- J1_sum / sqrt(theta * TP_sum)     # NOTE: square root in the denominator
  p      <- 1 - pnorm(z)                      # one-sided (upper tail)
  c(J1 = J1_sum, TP = TP_sum, z = z, p_value = p,
    crit_5pct = q95, reject = as.numeric(p < 0.05))
}

# (i) first 30-minute interval on 27 April 2026
row_i <- agg_30 %>% filter(date == as.Date("2026-04-27"), interval30 == 1)
test_i <- test_jump(row_i$J1, row_i$TP)

# (ii) complete sample
test_ii <- test_jump(agg_30$J1, agg_30$TP)

# (iii) final trading week: 27 April - 1 May 2026
last_week <- agg_30 %>% filter(date >= as.Date("2026-04-27"),
                               date <= as.Date("2026-05-01"))
test_iii <- test_jump(last_week$J1, last_week$TP)

# ---- Results table ----
test_tbl <- data.frame(
  Test = c("(i) 27 Apr, 9:30-10:00",
           "(ii) Complete sample",
           "(iii) Final week (27 Apr - 1 May)"),
  J1   = c(test_i["J1"],   test_ii["J1"],   test_iii["J1"]),
  z    = c(test_i["z"],    test_ii["z"],    test_iii["z"]),
  p    = c(test_i["p_value"], test_ii["p_value"], test_iii["p_value"]),
  Reject_5pct = c("Yes", "Yes", "Yes")
)
tab_fig(test_tbl, title = "Table 7. One-sided J1 jump tests (H0: no jump variation)",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 6, base_size = 9)
```

**Answer (b).** The test is the one-sided $J1$ jump test. Under $H_0$ of no jump
variation, $E[J1_t]=0$ and
$$\operatorname{Var}(J1_t)=\theta\,\Delta t\int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_s^4\,ds,\qquad
\theta=\frac{\pi^2}{4}+\pi-5\approx0.6089938,$$
where $\Delta t\int\sigma_s^4ds$ is the integrated quarticity, estimated by the tri-power quarticity
$$\mathrm{TP}_t=\Delta t^{-1}\mu^{-3}\sum_j|r_{t-1+j\Delta t}|^{4/3}
\big|r_{t-1+(j-1)\Delta t}\big|^{4/3}\big|r_{t-1+(j-2)\Delta t}\big|^{4/3},\qquad
\mu=2^{2/3}\Gamma(7/6)\Gamma(1/2)^{-1}\approx0.8308615 .$$
In the implementation the factor $\Delta t^{-1}$ is kept outside the accumulated sum, so the variance of the
accumulated $J1$ over a set of intervals is $\theta\sum\mathrm{TP}$ and the standardised statistic is
$$z=\frac{\sum J1_t}{\sqrt{\theta\sum \mathrm{TP}_t}}\ \xrightarrow{\ d\ }\ N(0,1)\quad\text{under }H_0 .$$
This is equivalent to the lecture-note form; only the bookkeeping of $\Delta t$ differs. Table 6 confirms that
each trading day contains exactly 13 thirty-minute intervals, with the first running from 9:30am to 10:00am,
as required.

The one-sided 5% critical value is $z_{0.95}=1.645$. Table 7 reports the results:

1. In the first 30-minute interval on 27 April, $z=3.446$, far exceeding $1.645$, with a one-sided
   $p$-value of $2.84\times10^{-4}$, far below $0.05$. We reject $H_0$: there is evidence of positive jump
   variation in this interval.
2. For the complete sample, $z=3.888$ with $p=5.05\times10^{-5}$. We reject $H_0$: there is evidence of
   positive jump variation over the whole sample.
3. For the final trading week, $z=6.636$ with $p=1.61\times10^{-11}$. We reject $H_0$, and this is the
   strongest evidence of the three.

All three tests reject the null of no jump variation, indicating genuine positive jump variation
rather than random noise. Although the final trading week contains only 65 intervals (versus 130 for the
complete sample), its $z$-statistic is the largest, meaning the evidence against the no-jump null is strongest
for the final trading week. It is worth noting that jump tests typically find
"too many jumps" — considerably more than can be matched to news events — and that practitioners therefore
often use the 1% level to compensate; at the 1% level all three tests here would still reject decisively.

## Question 2 (c)

```{r q2c}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2(c) Realized range volatility (RRV) vs realized volatility (RV)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# MOTIVATION.  RV uses only the first and last price of each interval.  The
# RANGE (highest minus lowest log price) uses the whole path inside the
# interval and therefore extracts more information about the same integrated
# variance, at the price of a scale correction gamma_{2,n}.
gamma_2_5   <- 1.4728
gamma_2_inf <- 4 * log(2)      # ~ 2.7726

# ---- 1-minute log-price and 5-minute interval index (1..78) ----
prices_1m <- prices_1m %>%
  mutate(lp = log(price)) %>%
  arrange(date, timestamp) %>%
  mutate(
    day_start      = as.POSIXct(paste(date, "09:30:00"), tz = "America/New_York"),
    mins_from_open = as.numeric(difftime(timestamp, day_start, units = "mins")),
    interval5      = pmin(floor(mins_from_open / 5) + 1, 78)
  )

# ---- Range within each 5-minute interval ----
range5 <- prices_1m %>%
  group_by(date, interval5) %>%
  summarise(maxlp = max(lp), minlp = min(lp), hl = maxlp - minlp,
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(hl2 = hl^2, interval30 = ceiling(interval5 / 6))

# ---- 30-minute realised range volatility ----
rr30 <- range5 %>%
  group_by(date, interval30) %>%
  summarise(sum_hl2 = sum(hl2, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(rr5 = sum_hl2 / gamma_2_5,
         rrinf = sum_hl2 / gamma_2_inf)

# ---- 30-minute realised volatility from 5-minute squared returns ----
rv30 <- prices_5m %>%
  filter(!is.na(interval30)) %>%
  group_by(date, interval30) %>%
  summarise(rv = sum(RV_contrib, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

vol30 <- rr30 %>%
  left_join(rv30, by = c("date", "interval30")) %>%
  arrange(date, interval30) %>%
  as.data.frame(row.names = NULL)

# ---- Table C1: summary statistics ----
stats_c <- rbind(summ_one(vol30$rr5,   "rr5"),
                 summ_one(vol30$rrinf, "rrinf"),
                 summ_one(vol30$rv,    "rv"))
tab_fig(stats_c, title = "Table C1. Summary statistics of rr5 / rrinf / rv",
        digits = 7, base_size = 8)

# ---- Table C2: autocorrelations up to lag 13 ----
acf_c <- rbind(get_acf_tbl(vol30$rr5,   "rr5",   lag.max = 13),
               get_acf_tbl(vol30$rrinf, "rrinf", lag.max = 13),
               get_acf_tbl(vol30$rv,    "rv",    lag.max = 13))
tab_fig(acf_c, title = "Table C2. Autocorrelations of rr5 / rrinf / rv (lag 0 to lag 13)",
        digits = 7, base_size = 8)

# ---- Table C3 / C4: CV and correlations ----
cv_tbl <- data.frame(
  Series = c("rr5", "rrinf", "rv"),
  Mean = c(mean(vol30$rr5,   na.rm = TRUE),
           mean(vol30$rrinf, na.rm = TRUE),
           mean(vol30$rv,    na.rm = TRUE)),
  SD   = c(sd(vol30$rr5,   na.rm = TRUE),
           sd(vol30$rrinf, na.rm = TRUE),
           sd(vol30$rv,    na.rm = TRUE)),
  row.names = NULL)
cv_tbl$CV <- cv_tbl$SD / cv_tbl$Mean

cor_tbl <- data.frame(
  Pair = c("rr5 vs rv", "rrinf vs rv", "rr5 vs rrinf"),
  Correlation = c(cor(vol30$rr5,   vol30$rv,    use = "complete.obs"),
                  cor(vol30$rrinf, vol30$rv,    use = "complete.obs"),
                  cor(vol30$rr5,   vol30$rrinf, use = "complete.obs")),
  row.names = NULL)

tab_fig(cv_tbl,  title = "Table C3. Mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 7, base_size = 9)
tab_fig(cor_tbl, title = "Table C4. Correlations between the three volatility measures",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 7, base_size = 9)
```

```{r q2c-acf}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Autocorrelation functions of the three volatility measures
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Lag 13 is the key horizon: with 13 intervals per day it corresponds to the
# SAME thirty-minute interval on the following trading day.  Identical panels
# for rr5 and rrinf are expected - a constant scale factor cannot change
# autocorrelations.
par(mfrow = c(3, 1))
acf(vol30$rr5,   lag.max = 13, main = "ACF of rr5 (range, gamma_2,5)")
acf(vol30$rrinf, lag.max = 13, main = "ACF of rrinf (range, gamma_2,inf)")
acf(vol30$rv,    lag.max = 13, main = "ACF of rv (5-min squared returns)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Answer (c).** The realised range volatility estimator is
$$\mathrm{RRV}_t^{N,n}=\frac{1}{\gamma_{2,n}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\big(h_{t_{j-1}}-l_{t_{j-1}}\big)^2,$$
where $N=6$ five-minute intervals make up each thirty-minute interval and $\gamma_{2,n}$ corrects the bias of the
range as a volatility estimator. Here $n=5$ one-minute observations lie within each five-minute interval, so
$\gamma_{2,5}=1.4728$; in the limit $\gamma_{2,n}\to4\ln2=2.7726$ and
$\gamma_{2,n}\to4\ln2$].

**1. Average levels.** Table C1 shows a mean of $9.5\times10^{-6}$ for rr5 and $5.0\times10^{-6}$ for rrinf;
their ratio is approximately $1.9$, which is close to
$\gamma_{2,\infty}/\gamma_{2,5}=2.7726/1.4728\approx1.88$. The difference in means between rr5 and rrinf
therefore arises entirely from the scale factor. The mean of rv
($1.29\times10^{-5}$) is higher than both, but the three estimators measure volatility in different ways
(range versus squared returns) and are not on a common scale, so the average levels cannot be compared directly.

**2. Persistence.** The ACFs of rr5 and rrinf are identical because the scale factor is a constant and does
not affect autocorrelation. From Table C2 both range measures the lag-1 autocorrelation is $0.513$; the ACF then declines
to $0.042$ at lag 6 before rising again to $0.528$ at lag 13. The realised volatility series shows the same
qualitative pattern with uniformly lower values (lag 1 = $0.286$, lag 13 = $0.308$) on the ACF graph.

The relatively high autocorrelations at lags 1–2 reflect short-run intraday volatility persistence, while the
renewed increase at lags 12–13 reflects persistence across trading days, since lag 13 corresponds to the same
thirty-minute interval on the following trading day — that is, the intraday (diurnal) periodicity . The range estimators display stronger persistence at both horizons, plausibly because they
exploit the maximum and minimum one-minute log prices within each five-minute interval and therefore incorporate
more intra-interval information than the return-based measure; the ACF alone, however, does not establish the
mechanism.


**3.Variance.** The theoretical result is 
$$\operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{RRV})\approx0.4073\int\sigma^4(s)\,ds
\quad\text{versus}\quad \operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{RV})=2\int\sigma^4(s)\,ds,$$
The range estimator has substantially lower asymptotic variance. All three series are strongly right-skewed
(skewness 3.416 for the range measures and 3.470 for rv) and fat-tailed (kurtosis 16.59 and 15.72).

**4. Sensitivity.** Since All three series are strongly right-skewed (skewness 3.416 for the range measures and 3.470 for rv) and fat-tailed, and each measure is built as a sum of squared quantities — squared returns for rv, squared five-minute ranges for rr5 and rrinf — a single extreme intraday move enters in squared form and can dominate the value for that day. 

**5.Precision.** Table C3 reports the coefficient of variation:
$$\mathrm{CV}(rr5)=\mathrm{CV}(rrinf)=1.228,\qquad \mathrm{CV}(rv)=1.408 .$$
On a comparable scale the CV of rv is about 15% larger than that of the range-based
estimators, indicating that either realised volatility is descriptively noisier in this sample, or Realized volatility has higher volatility.
To figure out does RV really has a higher volatility, From Table C4 we have correlations of $0.839$ between rr5 and rv and between rrinf and rv, indicating that the three estimators the same volatility variation and differ only in their degree of noise. Together
with the data from Table C3, we do have the evidence to prove that RV have a higher noise and thus realised range measures provide descriptive evidence of greater precision

# Question 3

```{r q3}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Long memory in realized variance: ARFIMA, HAR and an AR(10) comparison
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The realized variance series is known to display long memory, i.e. an
# autocorrelation function that decays hyperbolically rather than exponentially.
# Two ways of capturing this are compared:
#   (i)  ARFIMA(0,d,0), which estimates the fractional differencing parameter d
#        directly on log realized variance;
#   (ii) the HAR model, which approximates long memory using three horizons
#        (daily, weekly, fortnightly) and turns out to be a RESTRICTED version
#        of an AR(10), so the two can be compared with an F test.
dat <- read_excel("data/ass2_q3.xlsx", sheet = 1) %>% filter(!is.na(rv))

# ---- 1. ARFIMA(0,d,0) on log realized variance ---------------------------
# ARFIMA(p,d,q) generalizes ARMA by the fractional difference operator (1-L)^d.
# With p = q = 0 it reduces to  (1-L)^d log(rv_t) = a0 + v_t.
# The key parameter is d:
#     d = 0        -> short memory (ordinary ARMA)
#     0 < d < 0.5  -> stationary long memory
#     d >= 0.5     -> non-stationary
z_log <- log(dat$rv)
z_log <- z_log - mean(z_log)      # centre the series before estimation

fit_arfima <- fracdiff(z_log, nar = 0, nma = 0)
d_hat <- fit_arfima$d
se_d  <- sqrt(fit_arfima$covariance.dpq[1, 1])
z_d   <- d_hat / se_d
p_d   <- 2 * pnorm(abs(z_d), lower.tail = FALSE)

tab_fig(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("d estimate", "Standard error", "z statistic", "p value (H0: d = 0)"),
  Value    = c(d_hat, se_d, z_d, p_d)),
  title = "Table Q3.1. ARFIMA(0,d,0) for log realised variance",
  transpose = FALSE, digits = 6, base_size = 10)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. HAR variables
# ------------------------------------------------------------
df <- dat %>%
  mutate(
    rv_l1  = lag(rv, 1),  rv_l2  = lag(rv, 2),  rv_l3  = lag(rv, 3),
    rv_l4  = lag(rv, 4),  rv_l5  = lag(rv, 5),  rv_l6  = lag(rv, 6),
    rv_l7  = lag(rv, 7),  rv_l8  = lag(rv, 8),  rv_l9  = lag(rv, 9),
    rv_l10 = lag(rv, 10)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    rvd = rv_l1,
    rvw = (rv_l1 + rv_l2 + rv_l3 + rv_l4 + rv_l5) / 5,
    rvf = (rv_l1 + rv_l2 + rv_l3 + rv_l4 + rv_l5 +
           rv_l6 + rv_l7 + rv_l8 + rv_l9 + rv_l10) / 10
  ) %>%
  na.omit()

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. HAR model
# ------------------------------------------------------------
har <- lm(rv ~ rvd + rvw + rvf, data = df)
df$har_resid <- residuals(har)

har_coef <- data.frame(
  Term      = rownames(summary(har)$coefficients),
  Estimate  = summary(har)$coefficients[, 1],
  Std.Error = summary(har)$coefficients[, 2],
  t.value   = summary(har)$coefficients[, 3],
  p.value   = summary(har)$coefficients[, 4])
har_fit <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("R-squared", "Adjusted R-squared", "Estimation sample size"),
  Value     = c(summary(har)$r.squared, summary(har)$adj.r.squared, nrow(df)))

tab_fig(har_coef, title = "Table Q3.2. HAR model coefficients",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 6, base_size = 9)
tab_fig(har_fit, title = "Table Q3.3. HAR goodness of fit",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 4, base_size = 9)

write.csv(df[, c("rv", "har_resid")], "har_residuals.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Unrestricted AR(10)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
ar10 <- lm(rv ~ rv_l1 + rv_l2 + rv_l3 + rv_l4 + rv_l5 +
                  rv_l6 + rv_l7 + rv_l8 + rv_l9 + rv_l10,
           data = df)

ar10_coef <- data.frame(
  Term      = rownames(summary(ar10)$coefficients),
  Estimate  = summary(ar10)$coefficients[, 1],
  Std.Error = summary(ar10)$coefficients[, 2],
  t.value   = summary(ar10)$coefficients[, 3],
  p.value   = summary(ar10)$coefficients[, 4])

tab_fig(ar10_coef, title = "Table Q3.4. Unrestricted AR(10) coefficients",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 6, base_size = 9)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Test the HAR restrictions against AR(10)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
aov_res <- anova(har, ar10)
restrict_tbl <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c("F statistic", "df (numerator)", "df (denominator)",
               "p value", "Conclusion at 5%"),
  Value    = c(round(aov_res$F[2], 4),
               aov_res$Df[2],
               aov_res$Res.Df[2],
               round(aov_res$`Pr(>F)`[2], 4),
               ifelse(aov_res$`Pr(>F)`[2] < 0.05,
                      "reject H0", "cannot reject H0")))

tab_fig(restrict_tbl,
        title = "Table Q3.5. Restriction test: HAR (restricted) vs AR(10) (unrestricted)",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 4, base_size = 10)
```

```{r q3-acf}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# ACF of realized variance and of the HAR residuals
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# If the HAR captures the persistence, its residuals should show little
# remaining autocorrelation, whereas rv itself decays very slowly.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(df$rv,        lag.max = 100, main = "ACF of realised variance")
acf(df$har_resid, lag.max = 100, main = "ACF of HAR residuals")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Answer.**

**1. ARFIMA(0,d,0).** The general ARFIMA$(p,d,q)$ model is
$$\alpha(L)(1-L)^d\ln\sigma_t^2=\alpha_0+\theta(L)v_t,$$
where $\alpha(L)$ and $\theta(L)$ are the $p$-th order autoregressive and $q$-th order moving-average
polynomials. With $p=q=0$ we obtain ARFIMA$(0,d,0)$, $(1-L)^d\ln(\mathrm{rv}_t)=\alpha_0+v_t$, estimated on the
mean-centred log realised variance series. Table Q3.1 reports $\hat{d}=0.4830$, with
$H_0:d=0$ decisively rejected. Since $0<d<0.5$, the process is stationary and mean-reverting but exhibits long
memory: shocks to realised variance decay only hyperbolically rather than exponentially. The value $0.4830$
lies very close to the $0.5$ boundary, so persistence is extremely strong. For context, typical values of $d$ in financial applications lie between $0.35$ and $0.48$; the estimate here sits at the
upper end of that range.

**2. HAR model.** Using
$$\mathrm{rvd}_{t-1}=\mathrm{rv}_{t-1},\quad
\mathrm{rvw}_{t-1}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{j=1}^{5}\mathrm{rv}_{t-j},\quad
\mathrm{rvf}_{t-1}=\frac{1}{10}\sum_{j=1}^{10}\mathrm{rv}_{t-j},$$
the estimated model (Table Q3.2) is
$$\mathrm{rv}_t=1.471\times10^{-5}+0.4622\,\mathrm{rvd}_{t-1}+0.2832\,\mathrm{rvw}_{t-1}
+0.1077\,\mathrm{rvf}_{t-1},$$
with $R^2=0.543$ and adjusted $R^2=0.5417$ (Table Q3.3). The daily and weekly components are highly significant, while the fortnightly component is not
significant at the 5% level ($p=0.138$); together they explain about 54% of the variation in daily realised
variance. The residuals have been saved to `har_residuals.csv`.

**3. HAR restriction.** Expanding the HAR regressors and collecting terms:
$$\mathrm{rv}_t=\beta_0+\left(\beta_d+\frac{\beta_w}{5}+\frac{\beta_f}{10}\right)\mathrm{rv}_{t-1}
+\left(\frac{\beta_w}{5}+\frac{\beta_f}{10}\right)\sum_{j=2}^{5}\mathrm{rv}_{t-j}
+\frac{\beta_f}{10}\sum_{j=6}^{10}\mathrm{rv}_{t-j}+u_t .$$
Comparing with the unrestricted AR(10) (Table Q3.4), the HAR imposes
$$\alpha_1=\beta_d+\frac{\beta_w}{5}+\frac{\beta_f}{10},\quad
\alpha_2=\alpha_3=\alpha_4=\alpha_5=\frac{\beta_w}{5}+\frac{\beta_f}{10},\quad
\alpha_6=\alpha_7=\alpha_8=\alpha_9=\alpha_{10}=\frac{\beta_f}{10},$$
so the testable restrictions are
$$H_0:\ \alpha_2=\alpha_3=\alpha_4=\alpha_5\ \text{ and }\
\alpha_6=\alpha_7=\alpha_8=\alpha_9=\alpha_{10},\qquad H_1:\ \text{unrestricted AR(10)} .$$
Table Q3.5 gives $F(7,1022)=0.643$ with $p=0.7205$. Since $p>0.05$ we cannot reject $H_0$ at the
5% level: the restrictions implied by the HAR model are supported by the data. Consequently the more
parsimonious HAR specification is adequate — it reproduces the dependence structure of the unrestricted AR(10)
using 3 parameters instead of 10, and using the AR(10) would incur parameter proliferation without a
statistically significant gain in fit.

**4. ACF comparison.** The ACF of $\mathrm{rv}_t$ shows strong, slowly decaying positive autocorrelation. The ACF of the HAR
residuals is substantially smaller and mostly close to zero, indicating that the HAR model has removed a large
part of the persistence in realised variance. Nevertheless some residual autocorrelation remains at longer lags
(around lag 20), so the HAR does not completely capture the long-memory-like dependence — consistent with the
fact that a short-memory specification can only approximate a hyperbolic decay.

# Question 4

## Question 4 (a)

```{r q4a}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4(a) Raw vs diurnally adjusted transaction durations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Transaction durations show a strong INTRADAY (diurnal) pattern: trades arrive
# more frequently near the open and the close, and less frequently around
# midday.  `addurs` is the duration series after dividing out an estimated
# diurnal spline, so that the remaining variation can be modelled as a
# financial time series rather than a deterministic calendar effect.
dat4    <- read_excel("data/ass2_q4.xlsx")
dur     <- dat4$dur
addurs  <- dat4$addurs
timeadj <- dat4$timeadj
spline  <- dat4$spline

sumstats <- function(x) {
  c(n      = length(x),
    mean   = mean(x),
    sd     = sd(x),
    cv     = sd(x) / mean(x),
    min    = min(x),
    q01    = quantile(x, 0.01),
    q05    = quantile(x, 0.05),
    q25    = quantile(x, 0.25),
    median = median(x),
    q75    = quantile(x, 0.75),
    q95    = quantile(x, 0.95),
    q99    = quantile(x, 0.99),
    max    = max(x),
    skew   = skewness(x),
    kurt   = kurtosis(x))
}

ss_dur <- sumstats(dur)
ss_add <- sumstats(addurs)

q4a_tbl <- data.frame(
  Statistic = names(ss_dur),
  Raw_dur   = as.numeric(ss_dur),
  Adjusted_addurs = as.numeric(ss_add))

tab_fig(q4a_tbl,
        title = "Table Q4.1. Summary statistics: raw vs diurnally adjusted durations",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 4, base_size = 9)
```

```{r q4a-plots}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Autocorrelation functions of the raw and adjusted duration series
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Only the ACFs are plotted: their nearly identical shape shows that removing
# the intraday pattern changes the SCALE of the durations but not their dynamic
# dependence structure.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(dur,    lag.max = 100, main = "ACF of raw durations")
acf(addurs, lag.max = 100, main = "ACF of adjusted durations")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Answer (a).**

**1. Summary statistics.** Table Q4.1 shows that the raw durations have a mean of approximately
$30.11$ seconds and a median of $18$ seconds. The mean clearly exceeds the median, indicating a markedly
right-skewed distribution; skewness of $3.51$ and kurtosis of $25.96$ confirm strong right skewness and heavy
tails. The minimum is $1$ second while the maximum reaches $560$ seconds, so long trading intervals do occur; the
1% and 5% quantiles are both $1$ second, showing that a substantial proportion of intervals are very short.
These features match the standard stylised properties of transaction durations: durations are always positive and
very positively skewed, which is why the exponential (rather than a symmetric) distribution is the natural
starting point for the innovation.

The diurnally adjusted series has mean $1.18$ and median $0.76$; the mean still exceeds the median, so the series
remains right-skewed, but skewness falls from $3.51$ to $2.96$ and kurtosis from $25.96$ to $18.64$, while the
coefficient of variation falls from $1.217$ to $1.132$. Removing the intraday pattern therefore mainly changes
the scale and the shape of the distribution — it brings the mean close to one, as expected after dividing by a
diurnal spline — while reducing, but not eliminating, right skewness and heavy tails.

**2. ACF.** The plots show that both series display clear serial dependence: many autocorrelations
are significantly non-zero and predominantly positive. The ACF drops rapidly after lag 1 but then decays slowly,
which is suggestive of strong persistence and possible long-memory behaviour; the ACF alone, however, is not
sufficient evidence of long memory. The ACF shapes of the raw and adjusted series are almost identical,
indicating that although the diurnal adjustment changes the scale and some distributional features, it does
not noticeably change the dependence structure.

**3.** After using the diurnal adjustment to separate the “diurnal” aspect of the data from the “more financial” aspects, the ACF shows less evidence of long-memory autocorrelation but still significant correlation at short lags. Thus the adjusted duration still need to be modeled.

## Question 4 (b)

```{r q4b}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4(b) ACD(1,1) for adjusted durations, estimated by QMLE
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The Autoregressive Conditional Duration model writes the duration as
#       x_i = psi_i * eps_i,      psi_i = w0 + a * x_{i-1} + b * psi_{i-1},
# where psi_i is the conditional expected duration.  The structure mirrors
# GARCH, with psi_i playing the role of sigma_i^2 and x_i the role of r_i^2.
#
# ESTIMATION TRICK.  Because the exponential ACD is hard to fit directly, we
# exploit the formal equivalence with GARCH: setting mu = 0 and mapping
#       r_i -> sqrt(x_i),   sigma_i^2 -> psi_i,   u_i -> eps_i
# gives x_i = psi_i * eps_i^2 and psi_i = w0 + a*x_{i-1} + b*psi_{i-1}, i.e.
# exactly an ACD(1,1).  We therefore fit a ZERO-MEAN GARCH(1,1) with normal
# errors to sqrt(x).  Since the normal distribution is only an approximation to
# the exponential innovation, this is QUASI-maximum likelihood: consistent but
# less efficient than true MLE, so robust (Bollerslev-Wooldridge) standard
# errors are reported below.
dat_acd <- read_excel("data/ass2_q4.xlsx")
x <- na.omit(as.numeric(dat_acd[["addurs"]]))

# ---- Estimate ACD(1,1) as a zero-mean GARCH(1,1) on sqrt(x) ----
# Mapping: r_i -> sqrt(x_i), sigma_i^2 -> psi_i, u_i -> epsilon_i
spec11 <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model     = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
  mean.model         = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = FALSE),
  distribution.model = "norm"
)
fit11 <- ugarchfit(spec = spec11, data = sqrt(x), solver = "hybrid")

# ---- Coefficients with Bollerslev-Wooldridge robust standard errors ----
cf   <- coef(fit11)
rmat <- fit11@fit$robust.matcoef

idx <- function(p) grep(p, names(cf))[1]
est <- c(omega = as.numeric(cf[idx("omega")]),
         alpha = as.numeric(cf[idx("alpha")]),
         beta  = as.numeric(cf[idx("beta")]))

se_col <- grep("Std|SE|Error", colnames(rmat), ignore.case = TRUE)[1]
if (is.na(se_col)) se_col <- 2
se <- c(omega = as.numeric(rmat[idx("omega"), se_col]),
        alpha = as.numeric(rmat[idx("alpha"), se_col]),
        beta  = as.numeric(rmat[idx("beta"),  se_col]))

loglik11       <- as.numeric(likelihood(fit11))
persistence11  <- est["alpha"] + est["beta"]
se_persistence <- sqrt(se["alpha"]^2 + se["beta"]^2)
half_life      <- log(0.5) / log(persistence11)

psi11   <- as.numeric(sigma(fit11))^2    # psi_t = sigma_t^2 under the mapping
resid11 <- x / psi11                     # standardised residuals x_i / psi_i

# ---- Table: coefficients ----
q4b_coef <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("omega", "alpha", "beta"),
  Estimate  = as.numeric(est),
  Robust_SE = as.numeric(se),
  t_value   = as.numeric(est) / as.numeric(se))
q4b_coef$p_value <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(q4b_coef$t_value))

tab_fig(q4b_coef,
        title = "Table Q4.2. ACD(1,1) QMLE coefficients and Bollerslev-Wooldridge standard errors",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 6, base_size = 10)

# ---- Table: model summary ----
q4b_sum <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c("Log-likelihood", "Persistence (alpha + beta)",
               "Standard error of persistence", "Half-life (transactions)",
               "Sample size"),
  Value    = c(round(loglik11, 4),
               round(persistence11, 6),
               round(se_persistence, 6),
               round(half_life, 4),
               length(x)))

tab_fig(q4b_sum,
        title = "Table Q4.3. Fitted ACD(1,1) summary",
        transpose = FALSE, digits = 6, base_size = 10)

# ---- Save the objects needed by part (c) ----------------------------------
save(x, psi11, resid11, fit11, est, se,
     loglik11, persistence11, half_life,
     file = "acd11_results.RData")
```

**Answer (b).** The ACD(1,1) model of Engle and Russell specifies $x_i=\psi_i\varepsilon_i$ with
$$\psi_i=\omega_0+\gamma_1x_{i-1}+\omega_1\psi_{i-1},$$
where $\psi_i=E(x_i\mid I_{i-1})$ is the conditional expected duration and $\varepsilon_i$ is an i.i.d. positive
innovation. Estimation is by Quasi-Maximum Likelihood using the GARCH(1,1) representation:
setting $\mu=0$ and mapping $r_i\to\sqrt{x_i}$, $\sigma_i^2\to\psi_i$, $u_i\to\varepsilon_i$ gives
$x_i=\psi_i\varepsilon_i^2$ and $\psi_i=\omega_0+\gamma_1x_{i-1}+\omega_1\psi_{i-1}$, so an ACD(1,1) can be
estimated by fitting a zero-mean GARCH(1,1) with normal errors to the series $\sqrt{x_i}$.
Because the normal distribution is used only as an approximation to the exponential innovation, the estimator is
QMLE.

Table Q4.2 gives $\hat{\omega}=0.010307$, $\hat{\alpha}=0.042439$ and $\hat{\beta}=0.948735$, with
Bollerslev–Wooldridge robust standard errors of $0.001240$, $0.001563$ and $0.001379$ respectively. All three
coefficients are positive and highly statistically significant ($t=8.31$, $27.15$ and $687.89$). Table Q4.3
reports a maximised log-likelihood of $-26317.43$ and an implied degree of persistence of
$$\hat{\alpha}+\hat{\beta}=0.042439+0.948735=0.991174 .$$
This is very close to one, indicating very strong persistence and stationarity in the conditional expected duration.

## Question 4 (c)

```{r q4c}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4(c) Fitted expected duration and fitted trading intensity
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Objects saved by part (b) are reloaded here so that this section can be run
# independently of the estimation step above.
load("acd11_results.RData")

```

```{r q4c-plots}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Fitted expected duration and the implied trading intensity
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Trading intensity is defined as the reciprocal of expected duration,
# lambda_t = 1 / psi_t, so the two panels below are exact mirror images of each
# other by construction: long expected durations mean low trading intensity.
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

plot(psi11, type = "l", col = "steelblue",
     xlab = "Transaction",
     ylab = expression(hat(psi)[t]),
     main = "ACD(1,1): fitted expected conditional duration")
abline(h = mean(psi11), lty = 2, col = "red")

plot(1 / psi11, type = "l", col = "darkorange",
     xlab = "Transaction",
     ylab = expression(hat(lambda)[t] == 1 / hat(psi)[t]),
     main = "ACD(1,1): fitted trading intensity")
abline(h = 1 / mean(psi11), lty = 2, col = "red")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```

**Answer (c).** Comparing the two panels, the fitted trading intensity moves in the opposite
direction to the expected duration: when expected duration is high, intensity is low, and vice versa. This
inverse relationship follows directly from the definition of trading intensity as the reciprocal of expected
duration,
$$\lambda_t=\frac{1}{\psi_t},$$
so periods of unusually slow trading (long expected durations) coincide with periods of low trading intensity. The red dashed lines mark the sample averages of the two series, and the
mirror-image movement of the two plots is a direct consequence of this reciprocal relationship rather than an
additional empirical finding. The principal features of the fitted series are therefore: (i) pronounced
persistent swings between high-duration and low-duration regimes, (ii) no tendency to settle at the
unconditional mean for long, and (iii) a trading-intensity series that is the exact mirror image of the duration
series by construction.
